lead: Biofeedback instrumentation turns a small EEG or EMG voltage into a light or tone the patient can see or hear. The patient then tries to change the signal, for example to relax a muscle or to increase alpha waves. The machine does not cure by itself; it gives fast, clear information. Clinics use it for relaxation training, stress management, rehabilitation and some attention training. Some syllabi call this EEG biofeedback and EMG biofeedback. Only a few universities teach full loop design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for EEG and EMG signal bands and electrode placement, and Chapter 1.4 for bio-amplifier gain and common-mode rejection.

sections.h3: The feedback loop from electrode to patient

blocks.text: The chain starts at the patient. Surface electrodes pick up the tiny voltage. A high-gain amplifier raises it without adding much noise. A band-pass filter keeps only the EEG or EMG band. A rectifier changes negative and positive swings into one polarity by taking the absolute value. A smoother, a low-pass filter or averager, gives a steady envelope. A comparator compares this envelope with a set threshold. The output drives a tone or lamp. The patient hears or sees the result and tries again. This closed loop is the biofeedback mechanism.
V<sub>out</sub> = G × V<sub>in</sub>;  V<sub>env</sub> = average(|V<sub>out</sub>|);  C = 1 if V<sub>env</sub> ≥ T else 0
blocks.where: V<sub>in</sub> is the electrode signal in µV; G is amplifier gain, dimensionless; V<sub>out</sub> is amplifier output in µV; V<sub>env</sub> is smoothed envelope; T is threshold in the same unit as V<sub>env</sub>; C is comparator output, 1 for tone on and 0 for tone off.

items: Clean skin and attach electrodes over the target muscle or scalp site.
Amplify the small differential voltage with high common-mode rejection.
Filter to the chosen band and add a 50 Hz notch where needed.
Rectify, then smooth to form an envelope.
Compare the envelope with threshold T and drive the tone or light.
Adjust T as the patient improves, so the task stays possible.

sections.h3: EEG alpha training and EMG relaxation training

blocks.text: EEG alpha training uses scalp electrodes, often over the occipital region. The alpha rhythm lies in the 8–13 Hz band. The filter passes this band and rejects slower and faster activity. The threshold is set so the tone is on when alpha activity is above a chosen level. The patient sits quietly, often with eyes closed, and learns to keep the tone on. This is sometimes called alpha biofeedback. It is training, not a cure.

EMG relaxation training uses surface electrodes over a muscle such as the frontalis or forearm. The filter passes the EMG band, about 20–500 Hz, and rejects 50 Hz mains interference. The rectified smoothed signal is higher when more muscle fibres fire. The threshold is set just below the current resting level. The tone sounds when EMG is above threshold and stops when the patient relaxes. The silence is the reward. A physiotherapist may use this for tension headache or relaxation practice. The patient must understand the link between effort and tone.

Threshold choice decides the training. Too high a threshold gives no reward. Too low a threshold gives reward all the time. A good setting gives success often enough to keep the patient trying but not so often that the signal has no meaning.

Mains interference is a common fault. If an EMG unit also passes 50 Hz, the tone follows the mains hum and rewards interference, not muscle activity. Use a notch filter, short leads and good electrode contact. Motion, sweat and ECG pickup can also raise the envelope. Check the raw waveform before trusting the tone.

A comparator can chatter when the signal sits near threshold. Add hysteresis: turn on at a higher threshold T<sub>high</sub> and off at a lower threshold T<sub>low</sub>. Smoothing also reduces chatter. Feedback delay must be short. If the tone lags by seconds, the patient cannot link action to result.

Safety is still needed because electrodes touch the patient. Use an isolated patient circuit, low leakage current and a battery or medical-grade supply. Biofeedback is sensing only, not stimulation, but electrode impedance and patient current still need checks. Full loop design appears in only a few syllabi; most exams ask for the block diagram, one threshold calculation and the artefact list.

spec.title: Biofeedback loop
spec.aria: A block diagram of a biofeedback loop from patient to electrodes, amplifier, filter, rectifier, threshold and tone or light, then back to the patient.

examples.question: A surface EMG biofeedback unit has raw EMG 20 µV, amplifier gain 1000 and comparator threshold 15 mV. The rectifier gives absolute value and the smoother output equals the amplifier output for this steady test signal. Find the amplifier output in mV. Is the tone on? Give the comparator output as 1 for on and 0 for off.
steps: Compare: 20 mV > 15 mV, so C = 1 and the tone is on.
examples.answer: The amplifier output is 20 mV; this is greater than the 15 mV threshold, so the comparator output is 1 and the tone is on.
examples.check:
raw_uv = 20.0
gain = 1000.0
out_uv = raw_uv * gain
out_mv = out_uv / 1000.0
threshold_mv = 15.0
comparator = 1.0 if out_mv > threshold_mv else 0.0
print(out_mv)
print(threshold_mv)
print(comparator)

traps: Using gain without unit conversion: 20 µV × 1000 is 20 mV, not 20 V.
Letting 50 Hz through an EMG channel; the display then follows mains hum, not muscle activity.
Setting a threshold without smoothing; the comparator chatters when the envelope sits near T.
Confusing the EEG alpha band (8–13 Hz) with the EMG band (about 20–500 Hz).
Forgetting patient isolation: a sensing circuit still needs low leakage current and safe electrode current.

quiz.q: What does the rectifier do in a biofeedback loop?
quiz.a: It takes the absolute value, so negative and positive signal swings both add to the envelope.

quiz.q: What is the usual EEG alpha band?
Why is a band-pass filter needed before the threshold comparator?
quiz.a: It keeps the wanted EEG or EMG band and rejects 50 Hz and other activity, so the tone follows the chosen signal.

quiz.q: Raw EEG is 30 µV. Gain is 2000. Threshold is 40 mV. Find the amplifier output and state whether the tone is on.
quiz.a: V<sub>out</sub> = 30 µV × 2000 = 60,000 µV = 60 mV. 60 mV > 40 mV, so the tone is on.

quiz.q: Raw EMG is 10 µV. Gain is 1500. Threshold is 12 mV. Find the output and state whether the tone is on.
quiz.a: V<sub>out</sub> = 10 µV × 1500 = 15,000 µV = 15 mV. 15 mV > 12 mV, so the tone is on.

quiz.q: The tone switches on and off rapidly while the patient rests. Give two likely causes and one fix for each.
quiz.a: The envelope may sit near threshold, or 50 Hz may be passing. Fixes: add hysteresis and smoothing; add a 50 Hz notch and improve electrode contact.

quiz.q: Why must biofeedback feedback be fast, and how does a long delay affect training?
quiz.a: The patient must link an action to the tone. A long delay breaks this link, so the patient cannot learn which change turned the tone on or off.

quiz.q: In EMG relaxation training, why may silence be used as the reward?
quiz.a: The tone sounds when EMG is above threshold. Silence then means the muscle has relaxed below threshold, which rewards relaxation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wearable EMG patches and dry EEG headsets now use the same loop with phone apps. Research moves toward closed-loop neurofeedback and brain-computer interfaces. Search for alpha neurofeedback protocol, surface EMG biofeedback threshold, and patient isolation amplifier.
